w: Built on an earlier structure by hetman Jan Klemens Branicki, an 18th-century magnate who hoped to become king. Gardens, pavilions and sculptures modeled on French royal estates gave Bialystok its old nickname: Versailles of Poland, later softened to Versailles of Podlasie.
s: The palace behind Bialystok's old 'Versailles' nickname
_facts: Built by hetman Jan Klemens Branicki, 18th century
Modeled on French royal palace grounds
Gave Bialystok the nickname Versailles of Poland

w: Designed by Jozef Pius Dziekonski, this three-nave Catholic cathedral runs 90 meters long and seats 9,500 worshippers under twin towers reaching 72.5 meters. Seat of the Archdiocese of Bialystok, it was raised to basilica status in 1985 by Pope John Paul II.
_facts: Designed by Jozef Pius Dziekonski
90m long, seats 9,500
Twin towers 72.5m tall
Made a basilica in 1985 by John Paul II

w: Completed in 1913 to a design by Szlojme Rabinowicz, the Great Synagogue served Bialystok's Orthodox Jewish congregation until 27 June 1941, when Nazi forces set it ablaze with an estimated 700 to 800 people locked inside. Nothing of the building survives today.
_facts: Built 1913, designed by Szlojme Rabinowicz
Destroyed by arson on 27 June 1941
700-800 people killed inside

w: At 19 Warsaw Street, this cultural institution carries the name of Bialystok-born Ludwik Zamenhof. The city founded it on the mayor's initiative to mark the 94th World Congress of Esperanto, held here from 25 July to 1 August 2009 - a global gathering hosted in Zamenhof's own hometown.
s: Named for Zamenhof, host of the 2009 Esperanto Congress
_facts: Located at 19 Warsaw Street
Founded on the mayor's initiative
Marks the 94th World Congress of Esperanto, 2009

n: The Orthodox Cathedral of Saint Nicolas
w: Raised 1843-1846 on the site of an 18th-century Uniate church at Lipowa Street 5, this classical-style cathedral became the seat of the Bialystok-Gdansk Orthodox diocese in 1951. Since 1992 it has held the relics of Gabriel of Bialystok, an Orthodox saint, and it entered Poland's register of monuments in 1957.
s: Cathedral holding the relics of St Gabriel of Bialystok
_facts: Built 1843-1846 on a former Uniate church site
Cathedral of the Bialystok-Gdansk diocese since 1951
Holds relics of Gabriel of Bialystok since 1992
Listed monument since 1957

w: Officially the Church-Monument of Poland's Regained Independence, this modernist landmark by architect Oskar Sosnowski rose on St Roch hill between 1927 and 1946. It stands where a Catholic cemetery founded in 1839 was profaned by Russian forces during the January Uprising.
s: A church built as a monument to Poland's independence
_facts: Built 1927-1946, designed by Oskar Sosnowski
Official name: Church-Monument of Poland's Regained Independence
Stands on a former cemetery profaned in the January Uprising

w: Funded by Shmuel Cytron and completed in 1936 in the Modernist style, this former house of prayer at 24a Warynskiego Street survived the war for secular use and later became the Slendzinscy Gallery, an art gallery - a synagogue's afterlife as exhibition space.
s: A 1936 synagogue reborn as an art gallery
_facts: Completed 1936, Modernist style, funded by Shmuel Cytron
Served as an Orthodox Jewish house of prayer until WWII
Later became the Slendzinscy art gallery

w: Completed in 1893 at 3 Piekna Street in the Piaski district, this former synagogue was desecrated by Nazi occupiers in WWII, then reborn as a community center for Bialystok's remaining Jews until 1968. A 1989 fire ended that chapter; the building has held secular uses since 1995.
s: A 1893 synagogue that became a postwar Jewish center
_facts: Completed 1893 in the Piaski district
Desecrated by Nazis in WWII
Served as a Jewish community center until 1968
Fire in 1989, secular use since 1995

n: Monument to Orthodox inhabitants of Białystok who were killed and went missing in the years 1939–1956
w: A privately funded memorial remembers 5,000 Orthodox Christians from the Bialystok region who died in World War II and in the Stalinist repressions that followed it - a single stone accounting for a regional death toll spanning both the war and the peace that came after.
s: Memorial to 5,000 Orthodox war and Stalinist-era dead
_facts: Privately funded memorial
Commemorates 5,000 Orthodox Christians from the region
Covers WWII deaths and postwar Stalinist repression

w: A wooden synagogue funded by Jan Klemens Branicki - the same magnate behind Bialystok's Branicki Palace - stood here from 1703 or 1711 until Nazi forces destroyed it in 1939. It faced the Old Synagogue and the Great Synagogue across Bozniczej Street, a block once dense with Jewish prayer houses.
_facts: Built 1703 or 1711, funded by Jan Klemens Branicki
Destroyed by Nazis in 1939
Stood across from the Old and Great Synagogues

w: This 14.94-hectare green corridor threads through central Bialystok, linking Constitution of 3 May Park to Poniatowski Park - a continuous ribbon of trees and paths cutting across the city rather than a single bounded plot of green space to visit and leave.
s: A 15-hectare park linking two of Bialystok's parks
_facts: 14.94 hectares
Connects Constitution of 3 May Park and Poniatowski Park

w: Founded in 1938 by actor Aleksander Wegierko, this repertory theatre in Bialystok still bears his name today. A single performer's initiative from the interwar years grew into the city's standing drama company - a rare case of a theatre named for the actor who started it, not a patron who funded it.
s: A repertory theatre named for its 1938 founder-actor
_facts: Founded 1938 by actor Aleksander Wegierko
A repertory theatre company

n: Jewish cemetery in Białystok, Wschodnia street
w: Opened in 1891 after the old Rabbinic Cemetery closed, this walled 12.5-hectare ground holds roughly 6,000 matzevahs in marble, granite, limestone and sandstone, inscribed in Hebrew, Yiddish, Polish, Russian and German. It is the only Jewish cemetery surviving in Bialystok; the last burial was in 1969, closed in 1973.
s: 6,000 gravestones, Bialystok's only surviving Jewish site
_facts: Opened 1891, closed 1973
12.5 hectares, about 6,000 matzevahs
Inscriptions in Hebrew, Yiddish, Polish, Russian, German
Only surviving Jewish cemetery in Bialystok

w: Opened in 1968 and independent since 1976, this is the largest army museum in Bialystok's macro-region. Until the end of 2016 it ran the Siberian Memorial Museum as a branch - a reminder that Podlasie's military history includes deportations east, not only battles fought at home.
s: The region's largest army museum, once ran a Siberia branch
_facts: Opened 1968, independent institution since 1976
Largest army museum in the region
Ran the Siberian Memorial Museum as a branch until 2016

w: Modernized in the late 1990s and bought by Kompania Piwowarska in 2003, this brewery makes Zubr, one of Poland's most popular beers and now sold across Europe. At 6.0% ABV it is unusually strong for a Polish lager - a Bialystok brew punching above its home city's size.
s: Home of Zubr, an unusually strong 6% Polish lager
_facts: Modernized 1997-1999, bought by Kompania Piwowarska in 2003
Makes Zubr, sold across Europe
Zubr is 6.0% ABV, unusually strong for Poland

w: The largest parish in the Archdiocese of Bialystok, serving about 15,000 people, stands beside a monument to the Solidarity movement. An inscription reading '1981' on the outer wall marks the year the independent trade union was founded - politics carved directly into the church facade.
s: A church whose wall marks Solidarity's founding year
_facts: Largest parish in the Archdiocese of Bialystok, about 15,000 people
Solidarity movement monument stands beside it
Wall inscription '1981' marks Solidarity's founding
